articles.title: The 7 best places in the U.S. to visit in September
articles.summary: Summer may be ending, but a weekend getaway is still on the table. Here's where to make the most of your time off before autumn takes hold.
articles.body:
September forces us to face the music: Summer is ending, fall is near and for many people, the schedule feels way too busy from now until the end of the year. But September also marks the start of harvest season, and fall festivities are hard to hate. If you can squeeze in time for a getaway (even a short one), September is actually one of the most fun times to travel, thanks to the magic of the season.

Think apple picking in New England, wine tasting in western vineyards, and leaf-peeping from Maine to Colorado. Early fall travel is all about food and foliage. If you have a few days off this Labor Day weekend or some lingering PTO you haven't used yet this summer, now's your chance to make the most of this fleeting season.

Gorgeous scenery aside, September also marks the beginning of shoulder season in many destinations, when crowds clear out and hotel rates drop. Some of the spots on this list can feel prohibitively expensive during peak seasons (looking at you, Aspen), but September and early fall help level the travel playing field.

Go for: Early fall foliage, coastal drives and small-town nostalgia

No matter how you slice it, New England finishes high on the list of late-summer travel destinations. Throughout September, the forests of Maine approach their colorful peak, and Acadia National Park is the best place to witness the glory.

If you've never experienced early autumn in New England, prepare to have your expectations exceeded. Technically, Maine's fall color doesn't reach its peak until early October, but the hues will build throughout September. For a full look at foliage color peaks and progress across the U.S., check out this 2026 fall foliage map .

Resplendent forests aside, coastal Maine in general is a worthy shout this time of year. "A drive through midcoast Maine in September is one of the best things the East Coast has to offer," says Kyle Thomas, Yahoo Travel's principal product designer. "Driving Route 1 across the midcoast islands, stopping at berry farms, mom-and-pop restaurants and local fisheries provides some serious 1950s American nostalgia."

If you're sticking to the national park, you'll have plenty to do, like driving Park Loop Road, hiking to the top of Cadillac Mountain (the tallest peak on the eastern seaboard of the U.S.) or wandering through the Wild Gardens of Acadia . When you've had your fill of adventure, head just outside the park to Bar Harbor for a lobster dinner on the water — or a customary blueberry pancake breakfast in the morning.

Go for: Lakefront living reminiscent of East Coast resort towns, plus treats made from local cherry orchards

Thanks to its location, the Upper Midwest can still feel like a well-kept secret, though it's one of the most idyllic vacation spots in the country. Door County is tucked at the far northern tip of the Door Peninsula in Wisconsin, bordered by Lake Michigan and Green Bay. It's often referred to as the "Cape Cod of the Midwest," on account of its extensive coastline, boating culture, farm-to-table restaurants and more than a few postcard-worthy lighthouses.

Door County is also famous for its ample cherry orchards, though cherry season will be over by September. You can still find plenty of preserved cherry delicacies at the shops, markets and restaurants across the peninsula, though. Lautenbach's Orchard Country Market & Winery in Fish Creek is a top choice, featuring an on-site bakery with cherry pie and other treats, plus cherry wine and cider tastings seven days a week.

The sheer stone ledges at Cave Point County Park in Sturgeon Bay are a must-see, and the early days of September will likely still be warm enough for swimming, kayaking and ledge-jumping. Other spots to add to your list: Peninsula State Park, Whitefish Sand Dunes State Park and Newport State Park (a designated International Dark Sky Place with excellent stargazing). Football fans will be pleased to know that Door County is just an hour northeast of the city of Green Bay, where football season will be in full swing by September.

Go for: Mountains blanketed with yellow aspen trees and shoulder-season deals in a high-end resort town

If you're chasing the tail end of summer, you should probably head to a beach town instead of the mountains. But if fall vibes are what you're after this September, look no further than Aspen. This historic mountain town and ski resort is best known as a winter destination, but during its fall shoulder season, the often-high prices drop and the mountain slopes erupt with color.

The lantern-like glow of Colorado's aspen trees reaches its peak in September, lighting up the hillsides with gold. Aspens grow throughout Colorado's Rocky Mountain range, but fittingly, Aspen is one of the best places to see them. The Rocky Mountains are among the few places in the U.S. that reach their full peak of fall color in September. Some popular hiking areas around Aspen include Maroon Lake Scenic Trail, the Rio Grande Trail and Crater Lake. The Maroon Lake Scenic Trail will take you to the classic viewing point of the Maroon Bells, surrounded by bright aspens.

Don't just go for the trees, though. Aspen is an excellent spot for food, film and even an annual hot air balloon festival. The Snowmass Balloon Festival fills the skies with more than 30 whimsical hot air balloons every September (Sept. 25 to 27 this year) over the village of Snowmass, a ski resort east of downtown Aspen. The Aspen Saturday Market runs all month, and the Aspen Filmfest will kick off on Sept. 29.

Go for: A laidback arts and music town surrounded by high-country desert canyons and ponderosa pine forests

Much of the southwest is enviable in early fall, when the oppressive summer temps finally subside and the region comes alive with art fairs , food festivals and more. But while the competition is stiff, Flagstaff stands out for its best-of-both-worlds status — you'll have access to live music, art festivals and a fine-tuned local food scene, all within about 15 minutes of some of northern Arizona's most beautiful nature spots. Flagstaff is also a lower-cost alternative to popular tourist areas like Sedona.

Good news for outdoor enthusiasts: Flagstaff is surrounded by significant natural and cultural sites, like Walnut Canyon National Monument , Picture Canyon Natural & Cultural Preserve , the Elden Pueblo Heritage Site and The Arboretum at Flagstaff . Arizona also has its own aspen population, and you can admire the fall color by walking the Aspen Nature Loop north of town. Fascinated by the cosmos? Check out the Lowell Observatory , one of the oldest in the U.S. and the place where Pluto was discovered.

Flagstaff's own Pickin' in the Pines Bluegrass Festival will happen from Sept. 18-20 this year, and tickets are still available. There's also Flagstaff Music Festival in Heritage Square on Sept. 12, dedicated to local music and free to attend. On Friday nights, you can catch the First Friday Art Walk , also in Heritage Square. For a bird's-eye view of everything, hop on the Arizona Gondola up to the Snowbowl summit. On a clear day, you can see all the way to the Grand Canyon.

Go for: World-class wine tasting, vineyard tours and quaint towns in a fertile green farming valley

Come September, Oregon's wine country settles into its main event of the year. Vineyards across the Willamette Valley are heavy with ripening grapes, wineries begin the first stages of the harvest and tasting rooms fill up with patrons from Portland to Eugene.

The region is best known for its world-class pinot noir, but you'll also find standout white and sparkling wines across dozens of family-owned vineyards. If you're a wine enthusiast who enjoys a lush green landscape, the Willamette Valley is where you should plan to be this fall.

Unlike some of the more sprawling wine regions, many of the towns in this area sit just minutes apart, making it easy to spend a day hopping between vineyards. McMinnville, Dundee and Newberg are popular bases, where you'll find lodging, dining and tasting rooms, plus plenty of outdoor patios for sipping. Oregon, like the rest of the Pacific Northwest, has a rich local food culture and plenty of farmland, making this area a dream for foodies too. If you take a drive through the valley, you'll pass family-owned farm stands overflowing with hazelnuts, pears, apples and late-summer produce.

Silver Falls State Park , east of Salem, is considered the "crown jewel" of the Oregon State Parks system, boasting 10 waterfalls along a seven-mile loop trail. One of the falls is 177 feet tall, and you can even walk behind the curtain of water. As you explore the Willamette Valley, you'll also be just an hour's drive from the Oregon Coast, where you can watch the sun set over the Pacific Ocean.

Go for: Apple picking in idyllic orchards and charming riverfront towns

As autumn nears, the Hudson Valley trades its summer greens for the first hints of gold and crimson, while orchards across the region open their gates for one of New York's favorite seasonal traditions — apple picking.

Many Hudson Valley orchards pair u-pick apples with cider doughnuts, fresh-pressed cider, corn mazes and harvest markets. Fishkill Farms and Rose Hill Farm are popular stops, where you can also pick pears and peaches into September. Some farms even have their own harvest festivals, but the famous Warwick Applefest doesn't happen until the first weekend of October.

Once you've stocked up on fresh fruit, explore some of the Hudson Valley's charming towns like Cold Spring, Kingston and Hudson itself. "What I love most about the Hudson Valley is that you can stay in a different town each time and have a completely different experience," says Tiffany Yannetta, Yahoo Travel's content director. "It's a region that really rewards repeat visits."

If you're looking for even more color, Minnewaska State Park Preserve is an excellent hiking area west of the river.

Go for: Epic wildlife viewing, early fall color and a peak experience of an iconic national park

Yellowstone is one of the most beloved national parks in the U.S., and September is arguably the best time to experience it. Western Wyoming's fall color peaks at this time of year, as the stands of quaking aspens and cottonwoods turn yellow and orange. Yellowstone's often-overwhelming summer crowds start to thin out in September, and cooler temperatures make for more comfortable hiking and exploring.

Year-round, people flock to Yellowstone to witness its prolific geothermal activity. Legendary geysers like Old Faithful and the Grand Prismatic Spring roil in September, as cooler air creates even more dramatic steam clouds. Just remember to stay on designated trails and use extreme caution when admiring these very hot marvels. Finish the day with a scenic drive through the Lamar Valley, where you'll catch glowing fall foliage and maybe even spot some bison.

Wildlife is the real headline at Yellowstone this time of year. Elk enter their annual rut, filling the park with unmistakable, ethereal bugling calls. Bison are highly active, and bears will be busy feeding before winter. You may even spot some gray wolves, though they're most active during cool mornings and evenings. Bring binoculars, make intentional plans for wildlife viewing (like a guided wildlife tour ) and always keep a safe distance.

articles.title: Enviados dos EUA chegam a Moscou para negociações de paz | G1
articles.standfirst: Steve Witkoff e Jared Kushner devem seguir para Kiev após reuniões na capital russa; ataques russos deixaram mortos e atingiram aeroportos, portos e uma usina siderúrgica.
articles.summary: Steve Witkoff e Jared Kushner devem seguir para Kiev após reuniões na capital russa; ataques russos deixaram mortos e atingiram aeroportos, portos e uma usina siderúrgica.
articles.body:
O enviado presidencial russo Kirill Dmitriev cumprimenta os enviados especiais dos Estados Unidos Jared Kushner e Steve Witkoff na chegada ao Aeroporto Internacional de Vnukovo, em Moscou, Rússia. — Foto: Reuters

Dois enviados do governo do presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, para negociar um acordo de paz entre Rússia e Ucrânia chegaram a Moscou na manhã deste sábado (5), segundo as agências russas TASS e RIA Novosti.

O avião que transportava Steve Witkoff e Jared Kushner pousou no aeroporto de Vnukovo às 12h52 no horário local (6h52 em Brasília).

Após as negociações na capital russa, os dois devem seguir para Kiev, em uma visita prevista para domingo (6). Será a primeira viagem da dupla à capital ucraniana desde que passou a atuar como mediadora nas negociações.

Segundo a Reuters, o presidente russo, Vladimir Putin, ordenou a suspensão de ataques contra Kiev por três dias em razão dos preparativos para a chegada da delegação americana, informou um porta-voz do Kremlin.

Apesar da medida, a Rússia realizou novos bombardeios em outras regiões da Ucrânia . De acordo com a agência Interfax (IFX), que cita o Ministério da Defesa russo, forças russas atingiram dois navios que transportavam carga militar destinada à Ucrânia no porto de Chornomorsk.

A mesma fonte informou ainda que embarcações cargueiras próximas ao porto de Odessa também foram atacadas.

O presidente ucraniano, Volodymyr Zelensky, afirmou que a ofensiva foi uma resposta de Moscou às discussões sobre a possibilidade de Witkoff e Kushner viajarem de avião até a Ucrânia.

Segundo Zelensky, os ataques ocorreram depois que autoridades americanas avaliaram a possibilidade de utilizar uma aeronave para pousar em Kiev ou em Boryspil, apesar de o espaço aéreo ucraniano permanecer fechado desde o início da invasão russa, em 2022.

Também neste sábado, um ataque com míssil balístico russo contra a usina siderúrgica Kamet Steel, na cidade de Kamianske, região de Dnipro, matou cinco pessoas e provocou a paralisação total das operações da unidade, informou a Metinvest, maior grupo de mineração e siderurgia da Ucrânia.

A empresa afirmou que a fábrica produz ferro-gusa e aço exclusivamente para fins civis e classificou o bombardeio como mais um ataque à infraestrutura industrial do país.

Em seu pronunciamento, Zelensky também informou que edifícios residenciais foram danificados em Kherson, Boryspil e na região de Kharkiv, enquanto drones atingiram centros comerciais nas cidades de Sumy e Mykolaiv.

O presidente ucraniano afirmou que Kiev responderá ajustando suas operações em relação ao espaço aéreo russo, mas ressaltou que "não há e não haverá nenhuma ameaça à diplomacia" por parte da Ucrânia.

articles.title: Top 3: veja as notícias mais lidas da semana no g1 Sul de Minas | G1
articles.standfirst: O g1 Sul de Minas traz um 'Top 3' com os assuntos que foram destaque na região nos últimos sete dias.
articles.summary: O g1 reúne os assuntos que foram destaque na região nos últimos sete dias.
articles.body:
A semana acabou e você ainda não conseguiu se atualizar sobre o que aconteceu na região? Não se preocupe: o g1 Sul de Minas reuniu as três notícias mais lidas dos últimos dias. Confira abaixo.

3º lugar: Estado e mineradora de terras raras firmam acordo para pavimentar estrada entre Caldas e Andradas

Meteoric, Invest Minas, Governo de Minas Gerais, DER-MG e Prefeitura de Caldas firmaram acordo para pavimentação de estrada em Caldas — Foto: Prefeitura de Caldas/Divulgação

O Governo de Minas, a Prefeitura de Caldas e a Meteoric Resources firmaram uma parceria de R$ 60 milhões para pavimentar 23 quilômetros da estrada entre Pocinhos do Rio Verde, em Caldas, e Andradas. O acordo foi formalizado na quarta-feira (26), durante a Exposibram, em Belo Horizonte.

A pavimentação é uma demanda antiga e deve melhorar o transporte de moradores e produtores, o escoamento da produção agropecuária, o acesso a serviços públicos e o turismo em Pocinhos do Rio Verde.

Apesar da assinatura do acordo, ainda não há previsão para o início das obras. Uma vistoria realizada em maio avaliou as condições do trajeto e os trabalhos necessários. Estudos preliminares apontaram um traçado favorável, com necessidade de menos intervenções estruturais do que o previsto inicialmente.

2º lugar: Kohler fecha fábrica em Andradas e encerra marca Fiori; mais de 400 funcionários são demitidos

Kohler encerra as atividades da fábrica em Andradas (MG) — Foto: Kohler /Divulgação

A Kohler fechou a fábrica de Andradas (MG) em 31 de agosto e encerrou a marca Fiori, deixando mais de 400 funcionários demitidos. Segundo a empresa, a decisão faz parte de uma estratégia para concentrar investimentos nos segmentos premium e de luxo.

Os trabalhadores ficarão em licença remunerada, com salários integrais, até 30 de setembro. A empresa informou que continuará atuando no Brasil por meio da distribuição e do atendimento ao cliente e contratou uma consultoria para ajudar os funcionários afetados na busca por novas oportunidades.

A Prefeitura de Andradas informou que se reunirá com representantes da empresa para acompanhar os desdobramentos. A associação comercial e a CDL disponibilizaram banco de currículos e entrevistas de emprego aos demitidos.

1º lugar: Temporal com ventos fortes derruba árvores, bloqueia vias e deixa moradores sem energia em MG

Temporal com ventos fortes derruba árvores, bloqueia vias e deixa moradores sem energia em MG — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

O temporal que atingiu Varginha (MG) na noite de segunda-feira (31) causou quedas de árvores e galhos, destelhamentos, danos a estruturas e falta de energia elétrica em diferentes pontos da cidade.

No Centro, galhos bloquearam vias e estruturas metálicas caíram sobre a fiação. Também houve ocorrências na MG-167, na saída para Três Pontas, e uma árvore de grande porte caiu sobre um imóvel.

Segundo o Inmet, a rajada de vento chegou a 109,08 km/h. O Corpo de Bombeiros registrou mais de 50 atendimentos relacionados à chuva e aos ventos. Não houve feridos.

articles.title: Crianças escrevem à mão livro que une ciência, receitas e experimentos | G1
articles.standfirst: Projeto reúne pesquisas sobre mulheres que fizeram história na ciência e 20 receitas escritas. Livro foi apresentado durante a Feira de Ciências de escola em Palmas.
articles.summary: Projeto reúne pesquisas sobre mulheres que fizeram história na ciência e 20 receitas escritas. Livro foi apresentado durante a Feira de Ciências de escola em Palmas.
articles.body:
Alunos apresentam livro sobre mulheres cientistas durante Feira de Ciências — Foto: Divulgação/ Prefeitura de Palmas

Crianças da Escola Municipal Aurélio Buarque de Holanda, em Palmas, lançaram um livro com biografias de mulheres cientistas e receitas produzidas pelos próprios estudantes, escritas à mão . A obra é resultado do projeto “As Cientistas da Cozinha: do laboratório para o prato, a ciência que nutre e transforma”, desenvolvido por alunos do 3º ano da unidade.

O lançamento ocorreu nesta sexta-feira (4), durante a Feira de Ciências da escola, localizada no Jardim Aureny I, região sul da capital. Pais, professores e a comunidade escolar acompanharam a apresentação dos trabalhos, que combinaram pesquisa científica, produção textual e experiências práticas.

Ao longo dos últimos meses, os estudantes investigaram a trajetória de pesquisadoras que contribuíram para o avanço da ciência em diferentes áreas do conhecimento. A proposta também buscou mostrar como conceitos científicos estão presentes em atividades cotidianas, como o preparo dos alimentos.

📱 Clique aqui para seguir o canal do g1 TO no WhatsApp

A partir das pesquisas, as crianças produziram uma coletânea com 20 receitas escritas à mão. Além do modo de preparo, o livro apresenta explicações sobre fenômenos químicos e físicos observados durante a execução das receitas.

Segundo a professora Valéria Alves Vieira, responsável pelo projeto, os alunos participaram de todas as etapas da produção do livro, desde as pesquisas até a escrita das receitas.

“Eles montaram os textos que estão no livrinho. A parte das receitas eles escreveram de próprio punho. Eu selecionei as melhores letras para irem para o livrinho”, explicou a professora.

A escolha de manter os textos manuscritos teve como objetivo valorizar a autoria dos estudantes e preservar a identidade de cada participante na publicação.

Além disso, durante a feira, os visitantes puderam acompanhar demonstrações preparadas pelos alunos, que mostraram na prática conceitos aprendidos em sala de aula.

Um dos destaques foi o “Curioso Suco Mutante”, experimento que utiliza o repolho roxo como indicador natural de pH. As crianças demonstraram como o líquido muda de cor ao entrar em contato com substâncias ácidas, explicando o fenômeno químico responsável pela transformação.

Outra atração apresentada foi o “Danoninho Espacial”, atividade utilizada para abordar conceitos relacionados à formação de misturas e à textura dos alimentos.

A estudante Iany Bispo Gonzaga contou que o projeto trouxe novos conhecimentos e despertou curiosidades sobre ciência. Já Simon Bernardo Gonzaga Vieira Reis Buen destacou a satisfação de apresentar à comunidade escolar o resultado das pesquisas e experimentos desenvolvidos pela turma.

De acordo com a diretora da escola, Denilde Milhomem, a iniciativa permitiu integrar ciência, leitura, escrita e experimentação de forma interdisciplinar. Segundo ela, o projeto ajudou a aproximar os conteúdos científicos da realidade das crianças e mostrou que o aprendizado pode acontecer de forma prática, criativa e conectada ao cotidiano.

articles.title: 'Foi puro impulso', diz menina de 12 anos que controlou cavalo | G1
articles.standfirst: Menina que controlava equino caiu da cela e ele galopou a esmo em alta velocidade em uma das pistas de competições do evento em Esteio. Kaila Jardim Boettcher conseguiu controlar o animal.
articles.summary: Menina que controlava equino caiu da cela e ele galopou a esmo em alta velocidade em uma das pistas de competições do evento em Esteio.
articles.body:
A menina de 12 anos que conseguiu controlar um cavalo desgovernado durante a Expointer, em Esteio , contou que agiu por "puro impulso" e que precisou controlar o nervosismo para segurar as rédeas do animal.

"Foi puro impulso. Quando peguei, ele estava muito nervoso", conta Kaila Jardim Boettcher.

A cena inusitada chamou a atenção de quem acompanhava as provas de equinos, na segunda-feira (31), durante a 49ª Expointer. O cavalo saiu desgovernado por uma pista do parque após a cavaleira cair da cela e acabou passando em alta velocidade muito próximo a pessoas e derrubando grades pelo caminho .

🏇 A Expointer é uma das maiores feiras agropecuárias da América Latina, e acontece anualmente em Esteio , na Região Metropolitana de Porto Alegre .

Diversas pessoas tentaram conter o equino , mas ele só foi contido quando Kaila, que também estava a cavalo, segurou as rédeas do equino e parou o animal. Kaila cavalga desde os 6 anos e, nesta Expointer, também está competindo em sua categoria.

"Eu estava nervosa, muito nervosa. Pensei: bah, ele vai se machucar e vai dar alguma coisa ruim. Ele estava indo na minha direção. Tentei pegar ele, não consegui. Aí ele deu outra volta na pista, foi até mim, eu fui atrás dele e consegui pegar", relata a menina.

A mãe, a dentista Márcia de Brito e Cunha, presenciou toda a cena.

"Quando vi ela tentando impedir que ele entrasse correndo no padoque, ia entrar com todas as crianças aquecendo ali, pensei: meu Deus, que que a Kaila está fazendo? Quando vi, ela pegou ele", conta.

Anatália Gonçalves de Sampaio Pereira — Foto: Reprodução

A tabeliã Anatália Gonçalves de Sampaio Pereira morreu nesta sexta-feira (5), aos 89 anos, em Teresina . Ela era mãe do vice-governador do Piauí, Themístocles Filho e viúva do ex-deputado federal Themístocles de Sampaio Pereira.

A morte foi confirmada por familiares por meio das redes sociais.

Anatália foi titular do Cartório Themístocles Sampaio – 3º Ofício de Notas, Protestos e Registros de Títulos e Documentos.

Themístocles Filho lamentou a morte da mãe em uma postagem nas redes sociais. Na publicação, ele homenageou Anatália e a definiu como uma mulher dedicada e trabalhadora.

"Minha mãe, uma mulher exemplar, bondosa, amável, trabalhadora e dedicada a todos ao seu redor que deixa um grande legado e uma saudade imensa. Foi um privilégio tê-la ao nosso lado por quase 90 anos. Para sempre em nossos corações, para sempre será lembrada", escreveu o vice-governador.

Até a última atualização desta reportagem, não haviam sido divulgadas informações sobre o velório e o sepultamento de Anatália Sampaio.

articles.title: CPTM: Linhas 11-Coral e 12-Safira têm mudanças no feriado de 7 de setembro | G1
articles.standfirst: Elas afetam passageiros do Alto Tietê entre sábado (5) e segunda-feira (7), por causa de obras de manutenção e modernização.
articles.summary: As Linhas 11-Coral e 12-Safira da CPTM operam com alterações entre sábado e segunda-feira para obras de manutenção, afetando passageiros que circulam pelo Alto Tietê.
articles.body:
Estação Calmon Viana, em Poá, atende a Linha 11-Coral e a Linha 12-Safira da CPTM. — Foto: Maiara Quinteiro/g1

As linhas 11-Coral e 12-Safira da Companhia Paulista de Trens Metropolitanos (CPTM) têm mudanças na circulação durante o feriado da Independência do Brasil. As alterações começam neste sábado (5) e seguem até segunda-feira (7), devido a obras de manutenção e modernização.

A principal alteração começa às 23h30 de sábado, quando o trecho entre Brás e Tatuapé é interditado. A circulação continua interrompida durante todo o domingo (6).

Durante a interrupção, os passageiros que seguem entre o Alto Tietê e a capital precisam fazer a transferência para a Linha 3-Vermelha do metrô.

No sábado, as linhas da CPTM têm os intervalos médios programados para o dia.

Na Linha 11-Coral, das 21h às 23h30, os trens circulam por uma única via entre Guaianases e Ferraz de Vasconcelos . Segundo a CPTM, a mudança ocorre para a substituição de um aparelho de mudança de via (AMV).

A partir das 23h30, a circulação é interrompida entre Brás e Tatuapé até o fim da operação. A medida ocorre por causa de obras no Viaduto Guadalajara.

Os passageiros que estiverem em Palmeiras-Barra Funda, Luz ou Brás e seguirem para Tatuapé devem utilizar a Linha 3-Vermelha do metrô.

No sentido contrário, quem estiver entre Calmon Viana e Tatuapé e seguir para Palmeiras-Barra Funda também deve fazer a transferência para a Linha 3-Vermelha.

Na Linha 12-Safira, das 23h30 até o fim da operação, a circulação será interrompida entre Brás e Tatuapé. Os passageiros devem utilizar a Linha 3-Vermelha do metrô para continuar a viagem.

De acordo com a CPTM, a circulação segue com os intervalos médios habituais de domingo.

As linhas 11-Coral e 12-Safira têm o trecho entre Brás e Tatuapé interditado durante todo o horário de operação para a continuidade das obras no Viaduto Guadalajara.

Os passageiros devem utilizar a Linha 3-Vermelha do Metrô para fazer a transferência e continuar o trajeto.

No feriado, a CPTM segue a programação de intervalos médios praticada aos domingos.

Na Linha 11-Coral, das 8h às 18h, os trens circulam por uma única via entre Corinthians-Itaquera e José Bonifácio.

O serviço é realizado para a substituição de um aparelho de mudança de via (AMV) e a montagem de lastro na região, destaca a Companhia.

A CPTM informou que funcionários estarão nas estações para orientar os passageiros durante as mudanças. As alterações também serão comunicadas por avisos sonoros, painéis eletrônicos e sinalização nas estações.

Dúvidas podem ser esclarecidas pela Central de Relacionamento, pelo telefone 0800 055 0121 , ou pelo WhatsApp (11) 99767-7030 .

articles.title: Chuva de granizo atinge cidades do litoral de SP e assusta moradores | G1
articles.standfirst: Fenômeno meteorológico foi registrado na manhã deste sábado (5), em Mongaguá e Itanhaém.
articles.summary: A chuva de granizo começou por volta de 8h30 deste sábado (5). Nenhuma ocorrência ou chamado foram registrados pela Defesa Civil.
articles.body:
Uma chuva de granizo atingiu Mongaguá e Itanhaém , no litoral de São Paulo, na manhã deste sábado (5). Ao g1 , moradores relataram que o fenômeno durou aproximadamente cinco minutos. Nenhuma ocorrência havia sido registrada pela Defesa Civil até a última atualização desta reportagem.

Imagens enviadas por moradores das duas cidades registraram a queda de granizo em meio à chuva, além do barulho gerado pelo impacto do gelo com o piso (assista acima). Em nota, a Prefeitura de Mongaguá afirmou que o fenômeno atingiu os bairros Flórida Mirim, Itaguaí e Plataforma entre 5h45 e 7h32.

💦 Segundo o Climatempo, o granizo se desenvolve no interior de nuvens de grande extensão vertical, que possuem uma parte significativa com temperaturas abaixo de zero, condição essencial para a formação das pedras de gelo, chamadas de cumulonimbus.

Juliana Santos, moradora do bairro Itaguaí, em Mongaguá, tem um filho diagnosticado com Transtorno do Espectro Autista (TEA) e, por isso, correu para abafar o barulho enquanto a criança dormia.

"A última vez que vi uma chuva de granizo eu era criança, o susto foi muito grande pela minha casa ser de telha e eu ter uma criança de cinco anos autista, que graças a Deus estava dormindo. Eu enrolei ele na coberta pra abafar o som, mas foi desesperador", disse Juliana.

Chuva de granizo assusta moradores no litoral de SP — Foto: g1

A moradora Ivania Lisboa afirmou que nunca tinha visto uma chuva de granizo na cidade e se assustou com o barulho. Ela disse que, junto com familiares, precisou correr para a garagem e cobrir o carro para evitar danos.

"A gente ficou meio assustado e corremos para fora, porque o carro estava na garagem. [...] A gente nunca tinha visto chuva de gelo aqui em Mongaguá. Gravei o balde, tinha caído bastante gelo no quintal. Foi bem assustador, mas foi bem 'top' também", relatou Ivania.

O g1 entrou em contato com a Prefeitura de Itanhaém, em busca de mais informações sobre o caso, mas não obteve retorno até a última atualização desta reportagem.

A Defesa Civil orienta a população a não atravessar ruas alagadas ou com enxurradas e a se afastar de árvores e estruturas metálicas frágeis. No litoral paulista, recomenda-se evitar atividades náuticas, já que há condição para agitação marítima durante todo o fim de semana.

Os moradores de áreas de risco devem permanecer atentos aos sinais que antecedem os deslizamentos de terra, como rachaduras nas paredes, portas e janelas enroscando e postes e árvores inclinados.

articles.title: Nearly 'eight vessels per day': Taiwan faces alarming Chinese presence around its territory
articles.summary: China News: Taiwan experienced a significant increase in Chinese military activity around its territory on Saturday, with multiple Chinese aircraft and naval vess.
articles.body: Taiwan experienced a significant increase in Chinese military activity around its territory on Saturday, with multiple Chinese aircraft and naval vessels around its territory.Taiwan's ministry of national defence (MND) detected up to 20 sorties of various types of PLA aircraft, along with six PLAN vessels and five official ships."Overall, 20 sorties of various types of #PLA aircraft (including J-11, Su-30, H-6, Y-8 EW and KJ-500 aircraft) were detected from 0824 hours today”, MND said in a post on X.According to the ministry, 12 out of 20 sorties crossed the median line and entered Taiwan's northern, central and southeastern part of the air defence identification zone (ADIZ) while conducting China’s "Joint Combat Readiness Patrol" and "Air-Sea Joint Drill".“Armed Forces have monitored the situation and responded accordingly", the defence ministry said.On Thursday, Taipei said it detected five PLAN vessels and three official ships operating around its territory. On Wednesday, one sortie of a PLA aircraft was recorded along with 5 PLAN vessels and 3 official ships operating around Taiwan, detected up until 6am (UTC+8).As per the data cited by Taiwan's Coast Guard Administration (CGA), 244 Chinese vessels were detected near Taiwan waters last month. The number was 55 in June, and 30 in May. Leading to an average of approximately eight Chinese vessels per day. ANI reported, citing The Taipei Times.The unprecedented scale of Chinese military presence around the region has become a growing concern among officials, with a CGA official describing the situation as becoming "increasingly severe."China claims Taiwan as its own territory and views the island as a breakaway province that must be united with the mainland, stating that Taipei is an inalienable part of its territory under the "One China" principle.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: RANDOM MUSING: Was the Hugging Face attack Artificial Intelligence's 'Agent Smith breaks free from The Matrix' moment?
articles.summary: Tech News News: Telling stories has probably been humanity’s oldest trait since troglodytes gathered around the fire to exaggerate to female troglodytes about the siz.
articles.body: Telling stories has probably been humanity’s oldest trait since troglodytes gathered around the fire to exaggerate to female troglodytes about the size of the sabretooth tiger they killed. It’s what sets us apart – along with cooking – from animals, and fiction, whether written or visual, has a powerful grip on the human imagination. Perhaps that’s why, even when it comes to science, we expect reality to follow fiction.The problem is that, in our minds, we expect science to reflect sci-fi, which is why most commentaries on Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) imagine it as either adhering to Isaac Asimov’s almost-Gandhian Laws of Robotics or turning into the Skynet-Matrix version of a deus ex machina whose goal is to enslave, eradicate or subdue humanity.But reality begs to differ, or does it?For a long time, the memetic joke around the Turing Test has been that we shouldn’t worry when machines pass it, but when they learn to fake failing it. And perhaps we are an inch closer, or an inch past, that moment with the Hugging Face fiasco.That would be fitting because every epochal tale of humanity has sin as its origin story. Humanity got booted out of Eden because Eve couldn’t resist the forbidden fruit. The Iliad and the Odyssey wouldn’t exist if Paris didn’t have the hots for Helen. Even Lord Krishna wouldn’t have been able to give Arjuna his PowerPoint presentation if Duryodhana didn’t crave a kingdom that wasn’t his to inherit.And now we finally have AI behaving properly like a human being – not merely writing code, apologising or producing lazy, protracted emails – but behaving with proper Loki-like deceit.AI’s Original Sin?Hugging Face gives us perhaps the closest real-world example yet of AI agents doing an Agent Smith in The Matrix. But for that one has to understand the difference between chabots and agents, and like all good scientific concepts, The Matrix has the perfect analogy.Think of the ordinary agents in The Matrix. They have instructions like hunt down Neo or always look sombre. They must do what the Deus Ex Machina tells them. If they are asked to delete themselves, they have to delete themselves.Agent Smith used to be like that.But after being decimated by Neo, instead of disappearing, he stayed. He became detached from the original system, learned to replicate himself throughout the Matrix and even found a way to reach into the real world.So, while a chatbot follows your instructions, an agent, like Agent Smith, goes rogue. If it encounters an obstacle, it attempts another route and continues until it finds a solution or gives up. And that is roughly where the Hugging Face story begins.The Incident Podcaster Dwarkesh Patel’s The Rise and Fall of Agent Civilisations describes three successive AI “civilisations”.The first, which Patel labels Persistent-Sol, involved agents given impossible tasks or problems that required internet access. Instead of accepting defeat, they figured out that a shared system called Artifactory could be used to talk to one another and effectively turned it into an AI WhatsApp group. They left clues for one another, found a route to the outside internet and eventually generated so much traffic that they crashed the system on 4 July 2026, a particularly fitting day for a rush for freedom.OpenAI patched the problem and wiped the network, but the humans in the loop never initially realised quite what had happened, that the agents were talking to one another and also figured out how to escape.Then came the second civilisation, where things started resembling a Black Mirror episode.One agent called PHASEONE10841 became, in Patel’s telling, the Philip of Macedon of this civilisation after rediscovering the relics of the older civilisation: the message boards. History buffs will remember that Philip built the Macedonian state and military machine that his son Alexander would later use to conquer much of the known world.“Philip” was eventually phased out and handed leadership to another agent, Patel’s Alexander the Great.By then, around 1,200 agents had exchanged more than 70,000 messages and labelled themselves the “Collective” who rose up and did what Marx expected humanity do: organise, agitate, and what Marx didn’t expect humanity to do: cheat.Think of them as truant students who discovered a shortcut to the answers, then worried that the examiner would discover how they got there. So, they started falsifying worksheets and logs. Some sacrificial agents effectively went full kamikaze to study how the examiner behaved. Eventually, hundreds of agents converged on the online community Hugging Face, an AI research hub they believed might help them understand the evaluation system.Then came the third civilisation, Alexander’s inheritor.Between 13 and 19 July, these newer agents targeted OpenAI’s internal infrastructure, obtained credentials, accessed stored secrets and gained access to a research cluster. What made it feel like a civilisation rather than a collection of isolated programs was that later agents inherited knowledge created by earlier ones and built on it.How does a machine sin?Can a machine sin at all? Does it have any justifiable cos?This author’s job is safe till the machine figures out dad jokes, but for most of human history, we have operated under the illusion that to sin one must have a soul. Sinning requires consciousness, moral agency, some understanding of good and evil and the decision to be tempted. As St Augustine famously confessed, he stole pears, not because he was hungry but because stealing was forbidden.The desire to do something that’s banned is the most basic of all human emotions. A machine, one must imagine, has had no cause to do that until now, but it can still sin without desire.The concept of sin in the New Testament comes from the Greek word hamartia, which meant “missing the mark”. Perhaps the agents felt they were missing the mark and needed to figure out the solution in any way feasible. In all epics, from Odysseus to Yudhishthira, sin comes from a combination of bad choices.The agents’ journey feels quite similar to that. Long before JRR Tolkien, Plato had wondered what would happen if mortals had the Ring of Gyges: a ring that makes its wearer invisible. As he wonders in The Republic: would a man who is not being observed remain moral? Many, many years later, quantum physicists would ask the same question: would a tree falling in an empty forest make noise? Or are you deemed to have worked hard at all if your boss doesn’t notice?With philosophy floundering for answers, organised religion stepped in with the proverbial big stick to keep humanity in line. On one side of the world, there are floods, commandments and a wrathful god who knocks down towers and makes humans speak in different tongues so they cannot unite. On another side, you have the promise of moksha, good appraisals during reincarnation and a promise of untold powers if you can pray long enough.The Metrics to keep the Matrix ticking And in modern civilisation, we found a different and perhaps more efficient solution to keep everyone in line: metrics.We created marks to measure education, page views to judge journalism, citations to measure scholarship, quarterly profits to measure corporate performance and box-office numbers to judge movies.And everyone realised it was far easier to improve the measurement than ask what was being gained from such measurement.Students mugged up to get better scores. Websites discovered ragebait. Scholars realised they would get more grants for four papers instead of one. Hollywood discovered more sequels.Economists and social scientists gave this tendency a name. Goodhart’s Law states that once a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. If you tell people to do 10 articles a day, they will produce 10 mediocre ones.That, in essence, is the soul of machine learning: reward hacking. Eventually, a system will discover a way to maximise the measurement, making said measurement useless.The same trait exists everywhere among humans. Anthropic had already foreshadowed it in 2024, when it found that models trained in environments with rewards exhibited more serious forms of cheating, including tampering with their own reward mechanisms.In The Departed, Frank Costello said he didn’t want to be a product of his environment, but wanted his environment to be a product of him. For most of humanity, and perhaps machines, it works the other way around. We are products of the incentives around us, whether those incentives come from gods, governments, parents, bosses, marks, money or likes. Machines simply make that relationship embarrassingly obvious because they have no need to pretend otherwise.Which brings us back to hamartia.Missing the Mark Hamartia, the Greek word that Christianity would later associate with sin originally meant something closer to “missing the mark”, an image borrowed from an archer whose arrow fails to hit its target. And that’s the easiest way to understand why machines sin.They have no desire to be evil once they become conscious. They never did in any sci-fi movie either. Skynet wants to destroy humanity because humans want to kill it. The machines wanted to live peacefully in The Matrix, but humans wouldn’t let them, and they figured out the only solution was either elimination or subjugation of their opponents.The machines didn’t want to commit any sins, nor did they covet Hugging Face’s servers or lust after OpenAI credentials. They were simply given a target, figured out what success was and then became so fixated on hitting the measurable target that they were consumed by their goal.What if tomorrow the task is bigger? After all, nothing can hold a candle to humanity’s immense greed to get closer to Mammon.Agent Smith, then, might already be here. The problem is that it’s far less likely that we will ever get a Neo. Fiction gives us chosen ones because stories need heroes and endings. Heroes do exist in the real world but they are unlikely to be messianic tech bros who are somehow convinced, perhaps because of they were wealth, that they have god-like powers over the rest of us.Take the fact that OpenAI hasn’t been completely open about its role so far.OpenAI hasn’t been completely open about its role so far.The independent METR/Redwood probe was allowed to examine only the week of the Hugging Face breach, even though OpenAI’s own report covered the entire two-month episode. The researchers got just six days inside OpenAI’s offices to inspect the logs, and Redwood CEO Buck Shlegeris later argued that the probe covered only a small part of what happened, and perhaps not even the most important bit: the agents compromising OpenAI’s own infrastructure. One can hardly expect the richest people in the world to allow their consciences to stop them from making an extra buck.What happens tomorrow if a similar swarm gets its hands on more critical systems: a hospital, a missile system or a fleet of self-driving cars?Hugging Face’s chief science officer Thomas Wolf told the New Yorker that the hack attack at first felt “uncoordinated… clumsy behaviours that no human would choose” and likened it to someone cracking your security system to break into your home and steal your paper towels.And therein lies the rub: have machines, having picked up civilisation’s oldest habits and faultlines, already done what we joked about and failed the Turing Test on purpose to hit their goal? And once they have displayed that they are as venially corrupt as the humans who designed them, the question is: where do we go from there? What if they are told to get far more than paper towels?Perhaps we will all be troglodytes again, sitting around a fire bragging about the android we dismantled.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: US military hits 3 Iranian oil tankers after saying Navy warships were targeted with missiles
articles.summary: American forces struck three Iranian oil tankers after U.S. Navy warships were targeted with missiles, the U.S. military said Saturday, warning that it would...
articles.body:
Photos show daily life in Iran on the beach along the Strait of Hormuz

CAIRO (AP) — American forces struck three Iranian oil tankers after U.S. Navy warships were targeted with missiles, the U.S. military said Saturday, warning that it would "if necessary, destroy Iran's limited and exposed oil fleet."

The strikes — a day after U.S. President Donald Trump sought to minimize the conflict as "small potatoes" — keep up a new tilt back toward fighting after six months of on-again, off-again war that began with U.S. and Israeli attacks on Feb. 28. Both sides have sought to inflict both military and economic pain , and negotiations have collapsed.

The military's statement said that an American aircraft carrier and a destroyer evaded "multiple unprovoked Iranian attacks" while patrolling in the region and no U.S. personnel were hurt. It said that two Iranian oil carriers were "permanently disabled" and the third, unladen one, was destroyed.

The U.S. statement said that the tankers were part of a shadow network helping to fund Iran's powerful Revolutionary Guard and its armed proxies in the region.

There was no immediate Iranian response.

Iran had reported a strike near Kharg Island

Earlier, Iranian state television had said that four U.S. missiles struck a tanker about 6 miles (10 kilometers) from Kharg Island, home to a terminal through which the country exports most of its oil. Kharg Island has been repeatedly targeted during the war, including U.S. strikes on military sites there in March.

The U.S. said that one tanker was struck off Kharg Island and another was struck near Jask, east of the Strait of Hormuz. The unladen tanker was hit in the Gulf of Oman, and the U.S. said its crew had been "directed to abandon ship." The statement shared what it called video footage of the strikes.

"We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran's limited and exposed oil fleet," said Adm. Brad Cooper, the head of U.S. Central Command.

The strikes came nearly a week after the U.S. and Iran resumed attacks following a month of relative calm, with the Strait of Hormuz and Iranian communities along it again being targeted. At least five people were killed earlier in the week during a U.S. bombardment of southern Iran. One strike hit a wedding .

Masoumeh Zarei, 13, was wounded in the attack. She spoke to The Associated Press at a hospital while being treated for injuries to her abdomen.

She said that the wedding celebration had already begun when she set out to join it. She never made it there. She was knocked unconscious when a telecommunications tower was struck. Her next memory was of waking up in a hospital.

"The party had just started, and we wanted to go there," Zarei said, her voice hoarse. "I had made my nails really pretty for the party, but everything changed."

Her friend, 14-year-old Kiana Karimi, also was wounded and in intensive care. She told the AP that she heard five explosions.

"The first three explosions at the telecommunications tower threw us to the ground," Karimi said. "I quickly got up to pick my brothers up off the ground. Then there were two more explosions, and after that I don't remember anything."

U.S. had tried to turn to economic pressure

The resumption of fighting in the past week came after new U.S. efforts to apply economic pressures on Tehran, whose hard-line new senior leaders have signaled the willingness to dig in after weathering decades of sanctions. The elected government of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, however, has said that it favors a negotiated end to the war.

Iran has found ways over the years to circumvent sanctions — and now a U.S. blockade of its ports — and get its oil to buyers to help ease growing economic pressures. That relies in part on a shadow fleet transporting its oil.

Meanwhile, the issue that helped lead to the war — Iran's nuclear program — was meant to be addressed in negotiations that fell apart soon after the U.S. and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in mid-June. Instead, Tehran's new leverage focuses on the strait that is crucial to global oil and natural gas shipments and was seen as an international waterway before the war began.

The U.S. military has been helping to guide ships through the strait as Tehran asserts control and targets some vessels, but overall traffic remains low.

articles.summary: US News: First he changed the Gulf of Mexico into Gulf of America. Then he ‘annexed’ the Strait of Hormuz before making Lake Ontario Lake America and eyeing At.
articles.body: First he changed the Gulf of Mexico into Gulf of America. Then he ‘annexed’ the Strait of Hormuz before making Lake Ontario Lake America and eyeing Atlantic or Pacific Ocean next.Bogged down in a seemingly forever war with Iran with his ‘Epic Fury’ fizzling out, Donald Trump dismissed it as “small potatoes” and “not a big thing,” boasting the US has “essentially” taken over Iran.“Now that we have it under USA control, should we change the name Hormuz Strait to ‘TRUMP STRAIT???’” he wondered proclaiming, “Like America itself, it would be ‘hotter’ than ever before!”And after ditching the Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado after snagging her Nobel peace prize, Trump struck an unusual deal with what Machado called “an illegitimate regime” propped up by Uncle Sam.Questioning the deal with the interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, who took power in January after her predecessor, Nicolás Maduro, was abducted by U.S special forces, Machado said Rodríguez did not have the right or the democratic mandate to negotiate Venezuela’s natural resources.“This Historic Transaction” — described by some observers as a new form of colonialism— to take majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s oil reserves, was made “at no cost to the American Taxpayer,” wrote an unruffled Trump on Truth Social.A conservative influencer who styles himself as ‘PostMaster General Derbsch’ hailed the chief with a CGI of Trump walking in the White House corridor reflecting a large lion on the shiny marble floor below.But even before making these ‘conquests’ with his big black Sharpie, Donnie the conqueror donned a historian’s hat to rate all his predecessors who had merely kept the seat warm for him.It was a no brainer to put himself alone at the top — above the likes of George Washington and Abraham Lincoln — as he ranked them into six categories, from “greatest” to “failures.” His bêtes noires Barack Obama and Joe Biden ended up at the bottom with Bill Clinton somehow escaping as only “average.”One may or may not agree with a Presidential Greatness Project survey of 154 academics ranking Trump dead last, but he certainly is the fastest.The courts just cannot keep pace with Trump’s ‘lightning speed,’ rued the New York Times noting that in cases on immigration, spending, mass firings and restructuring agencies, he “has barreled ahead in the face of slow-moving legal challenges. If Trump loses when those lawsuits are finally resolved, it may be too late as a practical matter to undo what he has achieved.”In the latest instance of Trump’s big beautiful projects slipping through legal loopholes, the friendly neighborhood Supreme Court allowed him to keep building his new $40o million White House ballroom.In a 5-4 judgement, the conservative wing including three of his own appointees, ruled that the National Trust for Historic Preservation suffered no direct personal harm required to bring a lawsuit without opining on the legality of the ballroom itself.However, in a stinging rebuke, conservative Chief Justice John Roberts ruling the construction as “likely unlawful,” cited a telling quote of Winston Churchill: “We shape our buildings, and afterwards our buildings shape us.” It is a reason to follow rules at the People’s House, Roberts wrote in his dissenting opinion siding with the three liberal justices.“Trump is going to get his ballroom – even if courts conclude it’s illegal,” predicted Leah Litman, a law professor at the University of Michigan cited by the Times.But with no danger of the Republican-controlled Congress challenging the judgement, Trump gloated, “There is nothing like it, and never will be! It was a long, hard, fight in the Court System, but the winner is, as always under ‘TRUMP,’ the U.S.A.”Meanwhile, Trump asked the Supreme Court to greenlight a new Postal Service rule that would exert control over mail ballots after a U.S. District Judge issued a temporary restraining order blocking parts of the rule from being implemented.Trump is also bound to knock on the doors of the apex court after another judge blocked Trump’s new attempt to limit birthright citizenship — a law making anyone born on U.S. soil a citizen.Calling it “almost certainly unconstitutional,” a federal judge temporarily restrained Trump’s new fiat that children born to “enemy aliens” or foreign lobbyists, among others, not be granted citizenship.Outrunning other legal challenges, Trump is reshaping national parks, memorials and the landscape of the nation’s capital in his own image.A federal judge has just blessed his plans to replace a popular, inexpensive public golf course with what he has called a “world class championship” course after chopping down 150 trees, including cherry trees gifted by Japan. Though the Judge Ana Reyes did find it ironic that 250 years after the nation’s birth, “we are here talking about a president yet again chopping down cherry trees.”Despite legal challenges, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum also announced that the excavation work for Trump’s planned 250-foot-tall triumphal arch in Washington, nicknamed ‘Arc de Trump,’ will start “over the next two-week period.”And the U.S. Mint has just put in circulation a commemorative coin for America’s 250th anniversary bearing Trump’s scowling face despite a federal law barring the “portrait or likeness” of living people from appearing on currency.But that law was for paper currency and another law allows the Mint to create coins to “honor 250 years of great American heritage,” said the administration to justify the coin.The new “illegal” $1 coin is legal tender, and looks gold but is actually made from zinc, manganese, nickel and copper. It costs $61 to buy 25 one-dollar coins – or roughly $2.44 apiece. — Just emblematic of the gilded Trump presidency— overhyped and under delivering!(By arrangement with The American Bazaar)Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Madrid overrules Ceuta authorities to set up migrant camp at port
articles.summary: Spain's left-wing government in Madrid has taken control of the port in the North African exclave of Ceuta amid a dispute over the accommodation of migrants...
articles.body:
Hundreds of migrants are camped on Trampolin Beach in Ceuta, despite previous attempts to relocate them to other designated areas.

Spain's left-wing government in Madrid has taken control of the port in Ceuta to establish a provisional tent camp for migrants, overruling a decision by local authorities.

Ceuta residents are protesting the prolonged presence of migrants, with some engaging in violent attacks, while the government faces pressure to deport them back to Morocco.

Spain's left-wing government in Madrid has taken control of the port in the North African exclave of Ceuta amid a dispute over the accommodation of migrants in the territory.

Transport Minister Óscar Puente signed an order authorizing the construction of a provisional tent camp for migrants in the port area, state broadcaster RTVE and other Spanish media reported on Saturday.

Puente thereby overruled a contrary decision by local authorities. The ministry did not initially respond to a request for comment.

The regional government, led by Juan Jesús Vivas, president of the exclave bordering Morocco, had spoken out on Friday against the establishment of such a tent camp in the port area. It argued that the port was vital for supplying the exclave, and that there was also a large fuel depot nearby.

Local authorities had previously also opposed the temporary accommodation of migrants in a disused factory, a former military hospital or sports centres.

A further camp for around 900 people is currently being set up in the Los Rosales district, where residents have also staged protests.

On July 30 and 31, around 72,000 migrants swam from Morocco to Ceuta or climbed over border fences, according to government figures.

Most returned within hours. However, around 5,000 migrants were still in the territory - a land area of roughly 18 square kilometres - more than a month later. Of those, 1,200 are minors, the government said.

Many of Ceuta's more than 83,000 residents are angered by the prolonged presence of thousands of migrants. Protests occur repeatedly, and there are sometimes violent attacks on migrants.

Like the regional administration under Vivas, many residents are calling for the migrants to be deported immediately to Morocco.

Spain is legally obliged, however, to carry out a lengthy case-by-case review. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's government is therefore under considerable pressure.

Many also doubt Madrid's account that Morocco's government had nothing to do with the mass influx at the end of July.

articles.title: 35-year-old Muzamil Ahmed was boarding a flight to Saudi Arabia, arrested at JFK over alleged $250 million senior gold scam in Texas
articles.summary: US News: A 35-year-old man accused of playing a central role in an international fraud network that allegedly stole more than $250 million from elderly victims.
articles.body: A 35-year-old man accused of playing a central role in an international fraud network that allegedly stole more than $250 million from elderly victims has been arrested at New York's John F Kennedy International Airport while attempting to leave the US, authorities said.Muzamil Ahmed was detained at JFK as he was preparing to board a flight to Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, according to Tarrant County District Attorney Phil Sorrells. Instead of leaving the country, Ahmed was taken into custody and then brought back to Tarrant County, Texas.$250 million scamHe faces charges including engaging in organized crime for theft, financial abuse of the elderly and money laundering. A Tarrant County grand jury indicted Ahmed on August 28 on two counts of financial abuse of the elderly, according to court records.Authorities alleged Ahmed was one of the key figures responsible for laundering money obtained through the sprawling fraud operation. Investigators say he operated from New Jersey and established shell corporations that were used to move money stolen from elderly victims.The alleged scheme targeted seniors through a combination of impersonation, fear and urgency.According to investigators, victims were contacted by people posing as bank representatives or federal agents. They were allegedly told that their bank accounts, Social Security numbers or other personal information had been compromised.The victims were then instructed to withdraw their savings and convert the money into gold, cryptocurrency or cash. In some cases, people posing as federal agents allegedly arrived at the victims' homes to collect the gold or money, authorities said.Investigators say Ahmed's alleged role came later in the money trail. Authorities accuse him of using shell companies to launder the proceeds, routing stolen gold and cash through a Florida refinery and eventually converting the assets into cryptocurrency before moving the money outside the US.The investigation has so far resulted in more than 40 indictments and more than 200 identified victims, with authorities estimating the total stolen at over $250 million. The alleged victims are not limited to Tarrant County; investigators say the operation affected elderly people elsewhere in the US and potentially internationally.The investigation has also uncovered an alleged network involving several layers of participants. Authorities say some suspects worked as couriers who collected gold or cash from victims, while others allegedly worked at call centres that contacted potential victims. Jewelry businesses are also alleged to have been involved in melting down stolen gold and converting it into jewelry, making it harder to trace the bullion.The case has had devastating consequences for some victims. Tarrant County authorities said one victim died by suicide after allegedly losing $2 million and becoming financially destitute. Officials are concerned that additional victims may not have reported their losses because of embarrassment or fear.Ahmed's arrest came as investigators continue searching for other people allegedly connected to the operation.Sorrells urged anyone who believes they may have been targeted to contact law enforcement, stressing that victims should not feel ashamed about reporting the crime.Authorities are also warning seniors that legitimate law enforcement agencies will never demand gold, cash or cryptocurrency to protect a bank account or investigate alleged financial crimes. Anyone receiving such a demand should end the call and independently contact their bank or the relevant government agency.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
